screeningScope: Full-text source, eligibility, study-design, taxonomy, and synthesis-readiness review of queue positions 1-12 after Batch 03 publication.

decisionDefinitions.INCLUDE: Eligible for evidence extraction and synthesis after full-text review.
decisionDefinitions.DEGRADED: A required source or verification element was unavailable.

records.sourceFile: Association between intra and inter-limb strength asymmetry with sprint kinematics and force-velocity profile in youth team athletes.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Seventy-four youth football, volleyball, and handball athletes completed sprint, isokinetic-strength, sprint-kinematic, and force-velocity profiling. Strength-asymmetry relationships with sprint variables were weak to moderate and varied by metric; most athletes were below 15% asymmetry, while individual outliers reached 42%.
records.limitations: Cross-sectional associations cannot establish that asymmetry causes performance or injury outcomes. The mixed-sport youth sample, multiple asymmetry definitions and speeds, and absence of prospective injury or intervention data prevent a universal threshold or training prescription.
records.synthesisCaution: Treat asymmetry as test- and metric-specific descriptive information; do not turn 15% or any single value into a diagnostic, injury-risk, or training rule.

records.sourceFile: The impact of intrinsic foot muscle strengthening exercises in asymptomatic athletes with normal foot structure - A systematic review.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Four heterogeneous studies of asymptomatic athletes with normal feet reported improvements in intrinsic-foot-muscle strength and some morphological, motor, or propulsive-force outcomes. Meta-analysis was not possible; one study found no medial-longitudinal-arch stiffness change and running economy did not improve.
records.limitations: Only four studies were eligible, protocols and outcome units differed, risk of bias was present, and the small heterogeneous evidence base prevented pooling. Findings in healthy normal-foot athletes do not establish treatment effectiveness for pain, pathology, or injury prevention.
records.synthesisCaution: Present intrinsic-foot training as a plausible capacity option with low-certainty, outcome-specific evidence, not as a proven injury-prevention program or guaranteed running-performance intervention.

records.sourceFile: Prophylactic knee bracing in offensive linemen of the National Football League - A retrospective analysis of usage trends, player performance, a.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: NFL offensive-lineman seasons with at least 200 regular-season snaps from 2014-2020 were classified by observed brace use. Bracers had fewer major knee injuries than nonbracers (0.013 versus 0.049 per player; P=.04), with no cumulative performance-grade difference, while brace use fell from 16.3% to 5.6%.
records.limitations: Brace choice was not randomized, groups were imbalanced, prior knee history and baseline risk were unavailable, brace designs were combined, and brace and injury status relied on public images, video, and reports. Performance grades and player preferences leave substantial residual confounding.
records.synthesisCaution: Describe an association in NFL offensive linemen, not proof that prophylactic bracing prevents injury or has no performance effect for every player, brace, position, or level.

records.sourceFile: A comparison of rolling averages vs discrete time epochs for assessing the worst-case scenario locomotor demands of professional soccer match-play.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Twenty-five professional outfield players wore 10-Hz systems across 28 matches. Fixed epochs underestimated rolling-average peak total distance by about 7-10% and high-speed distance by 12-25%; peak values declined as epochs lengthened from 60 to 600 seconds and varied with position and match context.
records.limitations: The descriptive data came from one English Championship club and 28 matches, with device-, threshold-, epoch-, and context-specific estimates. Observed peak locomotor demand does not define the optimal training dose or account for every mechanical, tactical, or technical demand.
records.synthesisCaution: Use rolling averages with explicitly stated windows and thresholds for peak-demand description; do not compare values produced by different methods as if they were equivalent.

records.sourceFile: Accumulative weekly load in a professional soccer team - With special reference to match playing time and game position.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Twenty-four professional reserve-squad outfield players were grouped by match minutes and position while GPS-derived weekly load was accumulated across training and matches. Players with more match time generally accumulated more total, high-speed, sprint, and high-metabolic-load distance, with some position-specific patterns.
records.limitations: One professional reserve squad limits generalizability. Indoor training and internal load were not captured, match-minute categories concealed within-group exposure differences, and the observational design did not test whether compensatory loading improved performance or reduced injury.
records.synthesisCaution: Use match minutes and position to identify likely weekly exposure gaps, then verify with the athlete's complete external and internal load rather than applying the group pattern as a fixed top-up prescription.

records.sourceFile: Are elite soccer teams preseason training sessions associated with fewer in-season injuries - A 15-year analysis from the UEFA Elite Club Injury Study.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Across 244 team-seasons from 44 elite clubs, every 10 additional preseason sessions was associated with 22 fewer layoff days per 1000 hours, 0.18 fewer severe injuries per 1000 hours, 1.4 percentage points higher training attendance, and 1.0 point higher match availability.
records.limitations: Team-level observational data cannot establish causality or distinguish training exposure from team quality, player resilience, travel, roster, or medical-practice effects. Model fit was low (adjusted R-squared 1.3-3.2%), showing that most injury-outcome variation remained unexplained.
records.synthesisCaution: Protect sufficient preseason preparation, but do not translate the regression into a guaranteed benefit per session or chase session counts without considering content, progression, recovery, and player availability.

records.sourceFile: Introducing the Novel Deceleration Threshold Method - Comparative Reliability to Previous Sprint Deceleration Analysis Methods in Team‐Sport Athletes.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Ten women and 10 men completed three maximal 30-m sprint-to-stop trials on two days using a motorized linear encoder. The novel threshold method using the average of the best two trials showed excellent interday reliability for time to stop (ICC .93, CV 6.4%), distance to stop (.97, 5.3%), and average deceleration (.92, 7.1%).
records.limitations: The sample was small and mixed rather than sport- or position-specific, and the study evaluated reliability under one linear protocol and analysis pipeline. It did not establish criterion validity, injury prediction, responsiveness after intervention, or transfer to multidirectional sport decelerations.
records.synthesisCaution: Use the exact threshold, equipment, processing, and best-two-trial rule if adopting the method; reliability does not make the test a universal readiness or injury-risk measure.

records.sourceFile: Unilateral or bilateral standing broad jumps - Which jump type provides inter-limb asymmetries with a higher reliability.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Twenty-four amateur basketball players completed unilateral and bilateral standing broad jumps across two sessions. Most single-leg performance variables had acceptable absolute reliability, but asymmetry metrics were unreliable (ICC -0.40 to 0.58) and the direction of asymmetry showed mostly slight-to-fair agreement.
records.limitations: The small amateur basketball sample completed only two sessions, and conclusions depend on the chosen force-platform variables and asymmetry equations. Reliability of individual performance measures does not rescue the poor reliability of derived asymmetry scores.
records.synthesisCaution: Monitor raw limb performance before derived asymmetry, and do not use standing-broad-jump asymmetry from one session to label an athlete or make clearance decisions.

records.sourceFile: Validity of the Hawkin Dynamics wireless dual force platform system against a piezoelectric laboratory grade system for vertical countermovement jump variables.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Two recreational male soccer players performed 25 countermovement jumps each while Hawkin Dynamics platforms sat directly over Kistler platforms. Across 16 variables, differences were no more than 3.4% and 15 variables correlated .977-1.000, although fixed bias affected 6 variables and proportional bias affected 10.
records.limitations: Only two participants and 50 repeated jumps were tested in one session, so many observations came from the same individuals. High correlation does not equal agreement, and observed fixed and proportional biases can matter when interpreting small longitudinal changes.
records.synthesisCaution: The system appears suitable for the tested jump variables, but establish device-specific baselines and smallest worthwhile changes; do not interchange values with Kistler or ignore variable-specific bias.

records.sourceFile: Associations between skeletal muscle mass, fat-free mass, and saliva osmolality - A cross-sectional study.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: In 72 adults, skeletal muscle mass and fat-free mass measured by bioelectrical impedance were not meaningfully associated with MX3 saliva osmolality. Unadjusted and adjusted regressions were nonsignificant, and correlations were small (r=.10 and .08).
records.limitations: The cross-sectional convenience sample was not an athlete validation cohort; body composition used bioelectrical impedance, saliva was sampled twice within minutes, and hydration states and body-composition ranges may have been limited. Null association with body composition does not validate saliva osmolality for all hydration decisions.
records.synthesisCaution: Body size may not require automatic correction of saliva-osmolality values in similar adults, but interpret hydration from trends, context, and corroborating measures rather than one MX3 result.

records.sourceFile: The effects of integrative neuromuscular training on injury risk and athletic performance in athletes - A systematic review and meta-analysis.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: Twenty-five randomized trials involving 10,124 participants linked integrative neuromuscular training with lower injury risk (RR .73, 95% CI .58-.91) and improved jump, sprint, change-of-direction, and dynamic-balance outcomes (SMD .75-.97). Most outcomes were heterogeneous and most trials had some risk-of-bias concerns.
records.limitations: Interventions, athletes, sports, outcomes, and follow-up varied substantially, and most trials were rated as having some bias concerns. Subgroup findings about age, sex, football, frequency, and session duration do not establish causal superiority of those doses or groups; the local PDF is an unedited early-access manuscript.
records.synthesisCaution: Support multicomponent neuromuscular training while keeping program content, dose, adherence, population, heterogeneity, and evidence certainty attached to any effect estimate.

records.sourceFile: The Relationship Between Training Load and Injury in Athletes- A Systematic Review.pdf
records.evidenceSummary: This systematic review included 57 prospective studies across athletes, military, and first-responder populations; 47 reported at least partly significant load-injury relationships. Evidence was strongest for subjective internal load, while the direction of association depended on the load metric and timeframe.
records.limitations: The evidence was observational and highly heterogeneous in population, load definition, timeframe, injury outcome, and analysis; 15 studies were poor quality, 6 fair, and 36 good. Narrative synthesis cannot yield one safe workload threshold or prove that changing a monitored ratio prevents injury.
records.synthesisCaution: Monitor load as contextual exposure information and watch individual change, but do not use a universal ratio, threshold, or isolated workload value as an injury prediction or prevention rule.
